title: The Effects of Lighting Design on Mood, Attention, and Stress
research_question: To compare the effects of three lighting conditions (bright white light, dim blue light, and dim warm light) on mood, attention, and stress.

participants.description: Eleven 19-22-year-old students from Reed College (6 female, 2 non-binary, 2 non-binary women, 2 male). One participant's heart rate data was excluded, reducing N to 10 for that measure.
participants.recruitment: social media posts and word of mouth

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three lighting conditions in a lab setting: 1) SAD light therapy (10,000 lux, 6500°K, full-spectrum white light), 2) Blue light (50 lux, 450 nm light), 3) Control light (50 lux, 3500°K, warm incandescent light). Each exposure lasted 45 minutes.

measures.construct: Emotional state, Total Mood Disturbance, Depression-Dejection, Fatigue
Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) symptoms, Global Seasonality Score
Sustained attention, concentration, reaction time, omission errors, commission errors

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux, 6500°K white; Control: 50 lux, 3500°K warm; Blue: 50 lux, 450 nm blue)
findings.consequent: change in reported Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) from POMS-SF
findings.mechanism: The largest increase in positive mood in the control condition is possibly due to the less abrasive nature of the light. Both dim and a normative color, the control condition was also the most familiar to participants.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Total Mood Disturbance was not significantly different across light condition, F(2, 10) = 0.55, p = .58.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux, 6500°K white; Control: 50 lux, 3500°K warm; Blue: 50 lux, 450 nm blue)
findings.mechanism: the numeric pattern of the data indicates that the control condition was slightly less effective at reducing reported depressive mood than the SAD or blue light conditions, as one would expect if the SAD and blue light conditions were effectively reducing the symptomology of SAD
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Depression-Dejection was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) =0.089, p =.92.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux, 6500°K white; Control: 50 lux, 3500°K warm; Blue: 50 lux, 450 nm blue)
findings.mechanism: The Fatigue subscale unexpectedly showed the blue light condition as the least effective at reducing Fatigue in participants... in theory, the blue light should have reduced the production of melatonin and actually reduced feelings of fatigue
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Fatigue was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.14, p= .34.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux, 6500°K white; Control: 50 lux, 3500°K warm; Blue: 50 lux, 450 nm blue)
findings.consequent: change in heart rate from pre-session to mid-session
findings.mechanism: Heart rate at time two was typically lower than values at time one or time three (possibly due to the presence of the researcher at both time one and time three)
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that change in heart rate from pre-session to mid-session was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,9) = 1.49, p= .25.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux, 6500°K white; Control: 50 lux, 3500°K warm; Blue: 50 lux, 450 nm blue)
findings.consequent: change in heart rate from pre-session to post-session
findings.mechanism: this pattern implies a link between a slightly elevated heart rate and the control condition as compared to the SAD and blue light conditions.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that change in heat rate pre-session to post-session was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) =0.044, p= .96.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux, 6500°K white; Control: 50 lux, 3500°K warm; Blue: 50 lux, 450 nm blue)
findings.consequent: average reaction time in the Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: The average reaction time for participants' while they were in the SAD condition was higher than the reaction times in both the control and blue light conditions, indicating that in the SAD condition participants found it harder, or were less likely to have their full attention on the task.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that average reaction time during the CCPT was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.34, p = .28.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux, 6500°K white; Control: 50 lux, 3500°K warm; Blue: 50 lux, 450 nm blue)
findings.consequent: standard deviation of reaction times in the Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: numerically it appears that response times varied less in the blue light condition than in the SAD or control condition, potentially indicating a trend toward heighted (or more consistent) attention in the blue light condition
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that the standard deviation of reaction times during the CCPT was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.18, p= .33.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux, 6500°K white; Control: 50 lux, 3500°K warm; Blue: 50 lux, 450 nm blue)
findings.consequent: percentage of omission errors in the Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: The increase of omission errors in the SAD light condition indicates that participants were unable to commit their full attention to the task and, as a result, were less likely to respond to the target stimulus when it was presented.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that omission errors were not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 0.5, p=.62.

findings.antecedent: light condition (SAD: 10,000 lux, 6500°K white; Control: 50 lux, 3500°K warm; Blue: 50 lux, 450 nm blue)
findings.consequent: percentage of commission errors in the Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: it is possible that the reason for this discrepancy is that color discrimination, which was necessary for this task, could have been more difficult in the blue light condition because of the after-image left following the exposure to the blue light for 45 minutes.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that commission errors were not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 0.9, p=.42.

mechanisms: Bright SAD lamps' potential to distract and irritate participants.
Bright lights increasing arousal and physiological stress.
Blue light reducing melatonin production and feelings of fatigue.
Color discrimination difficulty in blue light due to after-images.
Subjective opinions/personal preferences for lighting conditions influencing psychological state more than photoreceptive ganglion cell effects.
Heightened mood influencing attention and stress levels (domino effect).
moderators: SAD susceptibility (SPAQ was administered as an exploratory co-variate, but no moderation analysis was reported).
Personal preferences for certain lights (discussed as a potential influence, not formally tested).
implementation_implications: Continue researching the effects of light on human behavior and cognition.
Careful analysis needed to determine best ways to evade negative repercussions of blue light from devices on mood and sleep cycles.
Further inquiry into lighting's effects in the built environment to increase productivity in offices or schools by modulating lighting for specific tasks.
Integrate modulated lighting for different tasks across different times of day into built environments to create optimal settings.
Small changes in lighting design, like switching lightbulbs, can create more comfortable and relaxing spaces, which is worth pursuing for subjective enjoyment.
limitations: Small sample size (N=11) leading to insufficient statistical power to detect genuine differences.
Experimental procedures potentially not sensitive enough or flawed.
Extraneous variables affecting data quality (e.g., non-uniform cloudy/sunny weather).
Participants completing sessions at various times of day, potentially masking stronger effects in the evening for blue light on circadian rhythms.
Study conducted during periods of varying academic workload (normal week, midterms, spring break), affecting participant stress and sleep patterns.
Measures potentially inappropriate for assessing constructs (e.g., CCPT for specific attention types, POMS-SF sensitivity and relevance of subscales/adjectives).
Participants potentially remembering and trying to maintain consistency in POMS-SF responses across repeated administrations.
Heart rate as a less precise measure of physiological arousal compared to cortisol or skin conductance, and easily influenced by researcher presence.
Possibility of a genuine null effect, implying previous literature may have erroneously reported effects due to methodological issues.
Subjective opinions and personal preferences for lighting conditions potentially influencing psychological state more than direct physiological effects.
Lack of participants predominantly diagnosed with SAD, potentially reducing the likelihood of observing mood, attention, and stress changes.

environmental_features: Blue light condition: 50 lux, 450 nm blue

instruments_used.name: POMS-SF
instruments_used.description: Profile of Mood States - Short Form, used to measure mood disturbance
